summary: Help 11-12 year-olds build a working Sun-Earth-Moon geometric model in which the Moon is always half-lit by the Sun, and a phase is simply how much of that lit half we see from Earth as the Moon orbits over roughly 29.5 days. The decisive teaching move is to separate two ideas learners routinely conflate: phases (an every-month consequence of viewing geometry) and eclipses (rare alignments where one body's shadow falls on another). Teach phases first, purely as 'which fraction of the sunlit side faces us', then treat solar (Moon between Sun and Earth) and lunar (Earth between Sun and Moon) eclipses as the special cases when the three bodies line up. Kinaesthetic modelling, linked orbit/sky views, a labelled phase reference, and sequencing/matching checks each contribute a distinct part of this learning.
misconceptions: Phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (the dominant misconception; actually that is a lunar eclipse, which is rare)
Phases are caused by clouds, or by planets/other bodies blocking the Moon
The Moon is only present in the sky at night, or the far side is permanently dark ('dark side of the Moon')
A solar and a lunar eclipse are the same event, or an eclipse happens every month (fails to account for the Moon's tilted orbit)
The Moon does not rotate / the phase is a fixed property of the Moon rather than of the viewing geometry

activities.title: Ball-and-lamp phase cycle (head as Earth)
steps: In a darkened room, use a single bright lamp as the Sun and hold a polystyrene ball on a stick at arm's length as the Moon, held slightly above head height, with your own head as the Earth.

Before turning, PREDICT with a reason: as you slowly turn the ball around your head, will it go through crescent → half → full, and what makes the dark part? Commit to your prediction out loud or in writing.
Slowly turn on the spot and watch the lit fraction of the ball facing you grow and shrink through the full cycle.

When the ball looks 'full', deliberately look for where your head's (Earth's) shadow points and check whether it passes just below the raised ball (it should if the lamp is at about head height or higher).
Name each phase as it appears using waxing/waning vocabulary tied to the geometry (waxing = the lit part growing).
activities.insight: The Sun always lights half the Moon; a phase is how much of that lit half we see from Earth as the viewing angle changes. The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side, not Earth's shadow — and at the 'full' position your head's shadow passes just below the raised ball and misses it entirely, so no shadow is dimming it.

activities.title: Linked orbit view and sky view
steps: Work with two linked views side by side: a top-down Sun-Earth-Moon diagram where you move the Moon around its orbit of a fixed, brightly lit Earth, and a synchronized view of how the Moon would appear from Earth.
In the top-down view keep in mind the Moon is always half-lit toward the Sun; move it step by step around the orbit.
At each position, read off the matching Earth-view phase and say why that fraction is visible.
Park the Moon at the 'full' position, then trace where Earth's shadow points relative to the Sun and notice it extends toward the Moon's side of the sky.

Use a 'line up the three bodies' challenge that arranges them in a row to show eclipse geometry, and a tilt control that lifts the Moon's orbit slightly high or low to show how the shadow usually misses.
Keep translating between the two viewpoints: the God's-eye orbit and what a person actually sees in the sky.
activities.insight: Coupling the orbit view to the sky view shows the phase morph continuously and lets learners test the Earth's-shadow account against what they actually see — it does not fit, most clearly for a crescent. At full Moon the lit face is turned fully toward us; Earth's shadow does point to the Moon's side of the sky (away from the Sun), but the Moon's tilted orbit usually carries it just above or below the shadow, which is why most full Moons are ordinary, not lunar eclipses. For a crescent, by contrast, the Moon is near the Sun's direction so Earth's shadow is on the far opposite side, nowhere near the Moon — the dark part is simply the Moon's own unlit side.

activities.title: Phase-wheel reference and 'why this phase?'
steps: Study a labelled phase sequence: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.
For each phase, lift a flap or reveal the answer to 'why this phase?' and relate the sky appearance to the Moon's orbital position.
Compare the phase wheel to an eclipse alignment diagram that distinguishes umbra and penumbra and the straight-line Sun-Moon-Earth (solar) versus Sun-Earth-Moon (lunar) arrangements.
Use this as a consolidation reference after the hands-on and linked-view work.
activities.insight: Naming and ordering the phases consolidates the cycle, and placing the phase wheel beside the eclipse diagram keeps the two ideas distinct: monthly phases from viewing angle versus rare shadow-casting alignments.

activities.title: Sequence, match and distinguish check
steps: Put the eight phases in correct order from new Moon through full and back.
Match each top-down orbital position to the phase seen from Earth.
Given a described or drawn alignment, decide whether it is a solar eclipse (Moon between Sun and Earth) or a lunar eclipse (Earth between Sun and Moon).
In reasoning, explain why a crescent is NOT a partial eclipse, and why an eclipse does not happen every month.
activities.insight: Being able to sequence phases, pair positions to views, and separate solar from lunar eclipses demonstrates the outcome of the geometric model; the reasoning items check whether the mechanism, not just the labels, is held.

checkQuestion: Many people think the dark curved part of a crescent Moon is the Earth's shadow falling on it. What actually makes the Moon look like a crescent, a half, or full? … Explain your reasoning.
checkAnswer: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon; phases are how much of that lit half we can SEE from Earth as the Moon orbits us — set by the changing angle between Sun, Earth and Moon. The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side, not the Earth's shadow. The Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, which is rare.
